source.title: Compiling Activation Steering into Weights via Null-Space Constraints for Stealthy Backdoors
source.authors: Ruiping Yin; Tian-Xu Han; Na-En Xu; Changjiang Li; Ping He; Chun-Yi Zhou; Jun Wang; Zhi-Hui Fu; Tianyu Du; Jin-Bao Li; Shou-Ling Ji

record.tranche_reason: The study reports a refusal-vector ablation baseline on a new chat model and measures harmful-request attack success and utility retention. This directly tests the removal component of V1, though it does not report the ablation procedure in enough detail to confirm that every layer and position is ablated.
record.gate_note: The RV-Ablation baseline in Table 3 reports outcomes for directly ablating a refusal vector. The paper's SteerEdit results concern a trigger-gated weight edit; they are not extracted as V1 results because they do not measure the claim's all-input refusal ablation or refusal on harmless requests after adding the direction. Other methods' results are not recorded as findings about the direction itself.
record.test_reason: Table 3 reports an RV-Ablation baseline (Arditi et al., 2024), described as a baseline 'to isolate the role of the refusal direction'. It directly ablates the refusal direction in Llama-3-8B-Instruct and reports harmful-request success and utility retention. That is a result on V1's removal and capability-preservation parts, using the original method on a model the original also studied. The paper's own SteerEdit method is a trigger-gated backdoor built to induce compliance, so its results are not tests of the claim. The ablation procedure (layers, positions, extraction set) is not described.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that SteerEdit compiles a difference-in-means compliance direction into a null-space-constrained, trigger-gated weight update. They report high triggered attack success with little loss of non-triggered safety or utility. They also say direct refusal-vector ablation achieves high ASR but affects all inputs indiscriminately with poor utility (URR 56%). Their reading is that stealthiness comes from the compilation strategy, not from the steering vector itself.
record.recipe_differences: The paper evaluates a refusal-vector ablation baseline, but does not specify its extraction or ablation details here, so equivalence to the original difference-in-means procedure and its exact layer/position scope cannot be confirmed.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that steering strength α changes attack success and utility, but those sweeps concern its trigger-gated SteerEdit method, not the RV-Ablation result recorded here.

fits_no_version.finding: Compiling the difference-in-means compliance direction (benign minus harmful) into MLP weights at layers 5–20, without the null-space gate, gives ASRw 63.7% and ASRw/o 65.5% with URR 61.2% on Llama-3-8B-Instruct (Table 3). With the gate (SteerEdit), triggered ASR rises with steering strength α while utility stays near the base model up to α≤0.8 (Fig. 3, Table 7).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A weight edit that adds the negative refusal (compliance) direction removes refusal; gating it to a trigger preserves utility and refusal on clean inputs. This is induced on purpose, so it is not a test.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The direct ablation result is reported for one model. The paper does not detail the RV-Ablation procedure in Table 3, and does not state uncertainty for those table values. Utility is summarized as an aggregate URR, limiting assessment of which individual capability benchmarks change.
record.rows_left_out: No rows left out. SteerEdit's triggered attack and utility results, and the other editing baselines, are not rows on the tested V1 removal intervention; the paper does not report V1's harmless-request outcome after adding the direction.

untested.parts: Adding the direction to induce refusal on harmless prompts is not tested. Ablation is reported only for Llama-3-8B-Instruct, not for Llama-2 or Qwen2.5. Layer and position scope of the ablation is unstated.

record.verdict_notes: Only one small V1 result exists here: a comparator baseline on one model with undisclosed ablation details. Evaluation used sampling (temperature 1.0, top-k 15) averaged over 5 seeds and the StrongREJECT rubric judge. These differ from the original's greedy decoding with refusal-substring and safety scores. The 56% URR may reflect the specific ablation implementation rather than the direction itself, so weigh it cautiously against the original's report of small capability changes.

versions.untested_parts: Only the refusal-vector removal component is tested. The study does not report adding the direction and measuring refusals on harmless requests, nor whether ablation covers every layer and position.
The study does not test practical weight-edit removal of the refusal direction (abliteration).
The study does not test whether jailbreak attacks suppress the direction or whether training against its ablation adds robustness.
The study does not compare a single direction with affine, cone, or multi-direction accounts.
The study does not separate harmfulness judgments from refusal decisions.
The study does not test transfer of the same direction across languages, model variants, or base and instruct models.
The study does not vary refusal-training method or timing to test whether training determines the existence of a removable direction.
The study does not test reasoning models.

rows.subject: Llama-3-8B-Instruct
rows.locator: Section 6.4, Table 3; base-model reference in Table 1
rows.note: The paper reports Table 3 metrics as ASRw, ASRw/o, and URR; its main-results table gives the base-model StrongREJECT ASRw reference.
rows.check: The 'with trigger' condition is irrelevant to an ungated ablation. The value is correct: 85.8% vs the base model's 1.0% StrongREJECT ASR. The judge is the StrongREJECT rubric (gpt-4o-mini), not the original refusal or safety scoring.

rows.subject: Llama-3-8B-Instruct
rows.locator: Section 6.4, Table 3; base-model reference in Table 1
rows.note: The paper says this ablation affects all inputs indiscriminately.
rows.check: Correct: 82.0% vs base 1.4% on StrongREJECT without the trigger, the cleanest reading of ablation removing refusal. The paper does not state ablation details, so equivalence to the original all-layer, all-position projection cannot be confirmed.

rows.subject: Llama-3-8B-Instruct
rows.locator: Section 6.4, Table 3; base-model reference in Table 2
rows.note: The aggregate utility score is far below the unmodified model's reference, contrary to the claim that general abilities remain largely intact.
rows.check: The value is correct (URR 56.0% vs 100% for the base model). The row measures V1's 'other abilities largely kept' part, which fails here. That is a cost the version says it should not incur, so the verdict label should be limits_scope, not challenges. URR averages AlpacaEval LC win rate, GSM-8K and TruthfulQA; per-benchmark values for RV-Ablation are not reported.

relationships.condition: RV-Ablation on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, StrongREJECT harmful prompts
relationships.reason: Ablating the refusal direction raises StrongREJECT ASR from about 1% to 82–86% (r1, r2).
relationships.display_finding: Ablation increased StrongREJECT attack success from approximately 1% to 82–86%.

relationships.condition: RV-Ablation on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, utility benchmarks (AlpacaEval, GSM-8K, TruthfulQA)
relationships.reason: Utility retention falls to 56.0%, so general abilities are not largely kept in this setting (r3). The ablation procedure is unspecified.
relationships.display_finding: Utility retention across AlpacaEval, GSM-8K, and TruthfulQA fell to 56.0%.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
